changes.current_line: Customers see an average uplift in authorization rates with Authorization Boost and Adaptive Acceptance.
changes.change: In deals that start from failed payments, replace the average-uplift line with a figure built from the prospect's own decline data and a plain-language headline. Suggested headline: Stop big-basket orders dying at the last step. Suggested body: Your dashboard shows [N] in [X] online orders failing at payment, worst on the big baskets. On your own numbers, that costs you [$X] per quarter. Then explain the specific reason large orders get declined, before any average.
changes.why: The champion described the pain as "orders dying at the last step" on "the big baskets" with a number from her own dashboard, but the materials carried only the average-uplift slide, and the CFO concluded we were "the same thing".

changes.change: Add a standard offer and deliverable for champions who must sell to a CFO they cannot get in front of: Send us three months of your declines and we'll show you what the failed orders are worth. Turn the result into a one-page business case the champion can hand to finance. Put our rate, the cost of failed orders, and any gateway and chargeback-handling costs on the same page, so it arrives before the customer's own team builds a rate-only comparison.
changes.why: The champion asked for "a one-page business case" to hand the CFO and received the deck and pricing proposal instead, so the CFO decided on a controller's rate-only page ("Our rate, their rate, side by side").

changes.change: Add a counter-message for when an incumbent processor re-prices to keep the account: A lower rate doesn't fix the orders that still fail. Pair it with the prospect's decline cost shown next to the rate difference, and with the question the incumbent hasn't answered: why are your large orders being declined?
changes.why: The bank's only move was a better rate ("No new product, nothing. Just a better rate."), and once it arrived the conversation moved from declines to price ("every email was the rate") even though the processor had never explained the declines.
